title: Established firms built much of the U.S. service economy by adding locations
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Immo Schott and Vladimir Smirnyagin find that the shift of U.S. employment towards services depended heavily on established firms expanding their networks. Between 1978 and 2023, service-sector employment increased by 71.5 million jobs in their Census Business Dynamics Statistics decomposition. About 37.6 million came from net employment growth at continuing establishments and 29.1 million from incumbent firms opening more establishments than they closed. Only 4.9 million came from net firm entry. A sector can therefore attract considerable entrepreneurial activity while most of its net job growth occurs inside businesses that already exist (figure 5 and appendix table A.3).

The distinction between a firm and its establishments changes the interpretation of scale. In 1979, service firms with at least 500 employees accounted for 41.6% of service employment. In 2023 they accounted for 55.3%, while representing under 1% of service firms. The average number of locations per large service firm rose from 18.8 to 32.5. In manufacturing the corresponding count stayed near eight. Smaller service businesses remained close to single-establishment operations. Health care and social assistance accounted for roughly 23% of service job gains, but several other subsectors each contributed more than a tenth. The change was broader than the expansion of any one industry (figures 3–4 and appendix A).

The accounting understates the eventual contribution of a newly opened branch to the extent that its hiring continues after the opening year. By definition, those later jobs go to continuing establishments. Attributing subsequent growth of young establishments within mature firms to branch creation raises its contribution from about 41% to over 54%. The same accounting caveat applies to entrants that survive and grow. Yet the authors’ tracking of four entry cohorts shows broadly stable total service employment as each cohort aged. Large gross startup and exit flows both matter. In the full decomposition new service firms created more than 98 million jobs at entry, while firm deaths removed roughly 94 million (appendix figures A.8–A.9 and table A.3).

The authors model two ways workers can move into services. Relative manufacturing productivity growth makes manufactured goods cheaper and shifts spending and employment toward services. In their free-entry framework this mechanism alone generates little change in the size distribution within services. A reduction in the incremental difficulty of opening and managing additional locations works differently. The most productive existing operators can replicate a successful establishment across many markets. Large firms already operate more locations in services, so a common change in expansion technology has a larger effect there. Information technology, logistics and more standardized processes are possible interpretations. The study does not identify which specific innovation lowered these costs.

In the joint experiment, calibrated to the relative goods price and the locations operated by large versus small service firms, manufacturing’s share of employment in the two-sector comparison falls from about 28% to 18.5%. The observed 2023 share was 9.6%. The model explains 51.5% of the historical decline. A productivity-only experiment accounts for 44.0% of the observed decline and a replication-only experiment for 16.7%. Those contributions do not add because relative prices adjust separately in each experiment. The share explained also depends on household demand assumptions. Removing the income-related shift in expenditure reduces the joint result to 26.4% (figures 8–11 and table 3). Establishment counts identify a channel of expansion that sector totals miss, but they do not reveal branch profitability or the returns earned by listed service firms.

questions.question: Which costs actually declined when established operators expanded into new locations?
questions.detail: The model represents easier replication through one parameter and treats technology, logistics and standardization as possible explanations. Consult historical company operating records, establishment-opening budgets and annual reports for comparable service chains. Track central overhead, branch setup costs and time to breakeven as scale increases. Distinguishing cost savings from stronger local demand would improve estimates of the return on further expansion.

questions.question: How much of incumbent expansion was organic in the industries most relevant to a portfolio?
questions.detail: Census enterprise size and establishment counts reveal rising concentration of employment. They do not identify the cash paid for acquisitions, new sites or leases. Match establishment histories and ownership changes to company acquisition disclosures and capital-expenditure schedules, separating mature networks from recent roll-ups. Similar growth in location counts could then be translated into very different financing requirements and margin paths.

questions.question: How sensitive is the historical attribution to the demand shift between goods and services?
questions.detail: The joint model explains around half the decline in manufacturing’s employment share, but the result changes when household spending responds differently to income. Examine the study’s expenditure-share regressions alongside underlying household expenditure surveys, sectoral price indexes and employment data for the same years. Testing the relationship separately across income groups and subsectors would help assess how readily the historical expansion extrapolates to a different demand environment.
